title: The Glass Cliff
text:
In 2003 an article in The Times of London claimed that companies with more women on their boards performed worse on the stock market. Michelle Ryan and Alex Haslam, psychologists at the University of Exeter, suspected the article had the story backward. Perhaps women were not causing poor performance, but were being appointed after it had already begun.

They looked at the companies in the FTSE 100, the largest firms on the London Stock Exchange, and identified those that had appointed new board members in 2003. Then they compared the share price performance of each company in the months before a man was appointed with the performance before a woman was appointed.

Companies that appointed women had, on average, been going through a period of consistently poor performance in the months before the appointment. Companies that appointed men had generally been more stable. Ryan and Haslam named this pattern the glass cliff: women were more likely to break through the glass ceiling into leadership when the position was risky and failure was more likely, which could then make them seem to blame.
lesson: Watch for who gets handed the hardest jobs and then blamed for the trouble they inherited. Judge leaders against the situation they were given.
source: Ryan, M. K., and Haslam, S. A. (2005). The glass cliff: Evidence that women are over-represented in precarious leadership positions. British Journal of Management, 16(2), 81-90.
caveat: Later studies found the effect in many but not all settings, and its size varies by context.
place: University of Exeter, Streatham Campus, UK
